sources.h1: Audio Matrix — Mini Boogee / Mini Matrix
sources.excerpt:
- **Archive parent:** Mini Boogee / Mini Matrix
- **Builder:** Audio Matrix / B.K. Butler
- **Catalog type:** Overdrive
- **Identity:** Early B.K. Butler tube overdrive/preamp sold under the Mini Boogee name and later renamed Mini Matrix after a request from Mesa Engineering. The two names refer to the same historical pedal family rather than separate circuits. [1][2]

Effects Database links Mini Boogee and Mini Matrix as the same pedal. Historical technical research by Kit Rae identifies the family as an early five-knob incarnation of Butler's Tube Driver work, made under the Audio Matrix brand from approximately 1980–1984, with two preamp tubes and no op-amps. [1][2]

Historical references document:
- **Five-knob architecture** on the Mini Boogee/Mini Matrix family.
- A **Bright** switch was part of the mini-amplifier-style layout.
- The circuit used **two preamp tubes**, not op-amps. [2]
Exact knob labels for every enclosure revision are not completely preserved in the accessible sources, so the archive does not invent a universal control legend.

- **Tube-based**, not transistor-only.
- **Two preamp tubes** are documented for the Mini Boogee/Mini Matrix family. Kit Rae's historical account identifies them as **12AX7** tubes. [2]
- No op-amp stage is documented for this family. [2]

- The defining distortion mechanism is the valve preamp circuit.
- No specific clipping-diode network is established in the reviewed historical sources.

Kit Rae documents multiple enclosure/name stages:
1. Bone-white cast-metal Mini Boogee, circa 1980.
2. Metal enclosure with imitation wood end panels, circa 1980.
3. Sheet-metal black/white version with wood end panels, circa 1981.
4. Essentially the same enclosure with the name changed to **Mini Matrix**, circa 1981.
Slight circuit and PCB changes occurred during production. The Mini Matrix name continued into the later part of the family's 1980–1984 production window. [2]

The name changed after Randall Smith of Mesa Engineering objected to the use of “Boogee” because of its similarity to Mesa's Boogie brand. The historical sources describe the resulting Audio Matrix label as **Mini Matrix**. [1][2]

- Historical accounts describe an **internal power transformer**.
- The product was hand-built by B.K. Butler under Audio Matrix.
- Exact mains specifications for every surviving unit are not established in the reviewed sources.

The Mini Boogee/Mini Matrix is an early Butler tube overdrive/preamp platform, preceding the later Tube Driver family. Historical descriptions emphasize its two-tube architecture and high-gain, tube-driven distortion rather than a conventional diode-clipping pedal. [2]

- **Same pedal identity under both names:** High
- **B.K. Butler / Audio Matrix attribution:** High
- **Two-tube / no-op-amp architecture:** High
- **12AX7 tube identification:** High
- **1980–1984 family history:** High
- **Multiple enclosure revisions:** High
- **Exact individual-unit tube/date codes:** Unknown
- **Exact diode topology:** Not established
- **Universal mains specification:** Not established

Effects Database was cross-checked against Kit Rae's detailed historical Tube Driver research and a surviving 1980s Mini Matrix/Boogee listing. The combined evidence establishes the naming history, approximate production period, multiple enclosure revisions, two-12AX7 preamp architecture and relationship to Butler's later Tube Driver designs. The archive keeps exact unit-level component details unresolved. [1][2][3]

1. Effects Database — Audio Matrix Mini Boogee: https://www.effectsdatabase.com/model/audiomatrix/miniboogee
2. Kit Rae — B.K. Butler Tube Driver versions/history: https://www.kitrae.net/music/Music_mp3_Tube_Driver_Versions.html
3. Reverb — Audio Matrix Mini Boogee 1980: https://reverb.com/uk/item/15569405-audio-matrix-mini-boogie-1980

sources.excerpt:
Tone Machines Blog: Audio Matrix Mini Boogee (1980) skip to main | skip to sidebar Pages Home Stompbox Collection On the Hunt About T.M. Contact Me The Super Fuzz Page Wednesday, December 21, 2011 Audio Matrix Mini Boogee (1980) ☟ Our friend Jerms just posted up another demo vid. of a mega cool (and rare) pedal, the Audio Matrix Mini Boogee . The Mini Boogee was the first offering from B.K. Butler of what was to become his legendary Tube Driver pedal. It was a badass overdrive with fuzzy tendencies that, in 1981 when he received notice from Randall Smith/Mesa decided to change the name to the "Mini Matrix" so no legal toes where stepped on. The pedal lasted until 1984 when it took it's final incarnation as the Chandler Tube Driver. There are technically 4 versions of the Mini Boogee, although all of them have the same pcb: version 1: White Bud Box - No Wood Panels - "Mini Boogee" 1980 version 2: White Bud Box - Wood Panels - "Mini Boogee" 1980 version 3: Black Bud Box - Wood Panels - "Mini Boogee" 1981 version 4: Black Bud Box - Wood Panels - "Mini Matrix" 1981-1984 Pictured above is the Mini Boogee from my collection, exactly like the one in the video. Another road we will travel down more deeply in the future, but know that it stacks amazingly with other pedals/fuzzes! My favorite combination is probably the Maestro MFZ-1 ( posted last week ) going into the Boogee. Pure Chunky Squelching Fire. Thanks for reading! -ed Posted by Ed Skymall at 10:22 AM Labels: Demo , Fuzz , Overdrive Email This BlogThis! sources.h1: Audio Matrix — Mini Boogee / Mini Matrix
sources.excerpt:
B.K. Butler Tube Driver Kit�s Secret Guitar, Gear, and Music Page Guitar stuff, gear stuff, soundclips, videos, Gilmour/Pink Floyd stuff, photos and other goodies. Copyright Kit Rae. VISIT MY SWORDS, KNIVES and FANTASY ART WEBSITE www.kitrae.net TUBE DRIVER HISTORY and VERSIONS Article written in 2015. Last update August 2020 For the main Tube Driver article CLICK HERE For the David Gilmour Tube Driver article CLICK HERE The Tube Driver was one of the first tube overdrives to enter the effects pedal market in the late 1970s. It became a very popular pedal among guitarists for the next 35 years, and onwards. Inspired by the Hammond organ sound of the band Deep Purple in the 1970s, the genesis of the Tube Driver happened when Brent K. Butler wanted to overdrive his keyboard by modifying the tube amplification circuit of an old stereo record player. He mounted the circuit in a Radio Shack enclosure and let a few local guitarists try it out. The positive response led Butler to further reduce and simplify the circuit, making an early version of his Tube Driver pedal for friends around 1975. After getting some practical work experience in electronics working for Carvin amplification, Butler refined the Tube Driver even more. He first marketed and sold them publicly in 1979, under the Butronics brand. They were housed in a blue metal box with 3 knobs and a 6AV6 or 12AV6 tube inside. He then made a 5-knob version called the Mini Boogee in 1980, sold through his Audio Matrix business that he ran out of Carvin's old building. He later changed the name to Mini Matrix after getting a cease and desist from Mesa Engineering, who owned the name Mesa Boogie. The Mini Boogee/Mini Matrix circuit included two 12AX7 preamp tubes. Butler then reworked the design again, combining an op-amp (operational amplifier or integrated circuit chip) and a pre amp tube running on starved voltage to generate the distortion, which led to the popular 4 knob Tube Driver. Butler says he designed that version in 1983 and it was produced in 1985. A rare original 1986 B.K. Butler/Chandler Tube Driver with TM after DRIVER and no B.K. Butler markings. Note the inout/output jacks are on the sides, rather than the end as on later models. A rare 1985 Butler/Chandler Tube Driver (left) and 1987 Butler/Chandler Tube Driver (right) Butler had trusted Chandler Industries to distribute some of his first tube pedals, the Mini Boogie/Mini Matrix, so he again used them for his new Tube Driver distribution in 1985. This was before Butler was actually marking pedals with his own name, so those first Tube Drivers were marked TUBE DRIVER™ and CHANDLER ELECTRONICS-PATENT PEND on the front, with LEDs placed above the the screen printed text. Butler decided he needed his name marked on the pedal. The second version was made with the LEDs moved below the text and were m arked TUBE DRIVER®, Concept & Design: B.K. Butler, with CHANDLER INDUSTRIES, INC at the bottom . In 1986, when he was still working for Dean Markely, Butler updated his tube overdrive design and added midrange knob. By 1987 he had resigned from Dean Markley and founded the Tube Works brand in Denver, Colorado. Some of his first TW products were the 5-knob Real Tube overdrive (TW-901) and Blue Tube Enhancer (TW-903, a lower gain version for blues players). These were essentially improved, 5 knob versions of the Tube Driver circuit under his own company name. A Tube Works magazine ad from the late 1980s, and the Dean Markley Overlord, which was a knockoff of the Tube Works Real Tube pedal Butler ended his relationship with Chandler Industries in 1987, but unfortunately Chandler had trademarked the name Tube Driver and Real Tube Overdrive the same year. They went on to have an inaccurate copy of the Tube Driver made around 1988. Then Butler's former employer, Dean Markley, made an exact clone of Butler's 5 knob Real Tube in 1988 called the Overlord.
